Categories of an Object’s Methods:
  Accessors (Inspectors) – methods that retrieve information from the object, Include getters
  Mutators – methods that modify the object’s state, , Include setters
  Combinators – methods that combine this object with others to produce a result, Does not modify current object
  Comparators – methods that compare objects (e.g., equals, compareTo)
  Predicates – methods that test a condition and return a Boolean (isDigit...)
  Transformers (Converters) – methods that produce a transformed version of the object or its data (toString)

Procedural programming is about writing procedures or methods that perform operations on the data, while object-oriented programming is about creating objects that contain both data and methods.
Advantages:
OOP is faster and easier to execute
OOP provides a clear structure for the programs
OOP helps to keep the Java code DRY "Don't Repeat Yourself", and makes the code easier to maintain, modify and debug
OOP makes it possible to create full reusable applications with less code and shorter development time

Syfte:Att bestämma systemkraven, att skapa en systemdesign utan väsentliga osäkerheter, (att förstå ett system, dess omgivning och villkoren för dess implementering)
Objektorienterad design (Objekt, tillstånd och beteende): mer generella begrepp, lämpliga att beskriva flesta fenomen som uttrycks i naturligt språk (objekt som substantiv, beteende som verb) jämfört med funktion, data och dataflöde
- Tydlig information om systemets omgivning, individuell problemlösning, kommunikation och samordning (även distribuera specialiserade data i organisationen) jämfört med (tidiga system med automatisera arbetskrävande informationsbehandlingsuppgifter)
- Nära sambandet mellan objektorienterad analys, objektorienterad design, objektorienterad användargränssnitt och objektorienterad programmering -> modellera sociala, ekonomiska och organisatoriska tillstånd (systemens gränssnitt, funktioner, processor, komponenter), (Analysen: objekt för att bestämma systemkraven, designen objekt för att bestämma själva systemet)

Begrepp: 
Objekt: En entitet med identitet, tillstånd och beteende (Mest grundläggande byggsten, Analysobjekt: abstraktion av fenomen i systemets omgivning (fenomen utanför systemet och är vanligen oberoende av varandra), Designobjekt: en del av systemet e.g. en kund) (fenomen inom systemet som kan utföras)
Identiteten hos ett analysobjekt uttrycker hur användaren skiljer det från de andra objekten i omgivningen
Identiteten hos ett designobjekt uttrycker hur andra objekt i systemet kan känna igen det, och därigenom få åtkomst till det. Designen ger också upphov till nya klasser

I analysen uttrycks objektets beteende genom de händelser som det deltar i eller upplever (e.g. kundobjekt inblandning i beställning/frakt av gods) -> hjälper att förstå hur och när systemets representation av ett objekt ska förändras
I designen uttrycks objektets beteende genom operationer den kan utföra och tillgängliga för andra objekt i systemet (e.g. lägg till beställning, ta bort beställning) -> låter systemet uppdatera tillståndet hos kundobjekt när fysiska världen förändras, inkapslar den interna representationen av objektets tillstånd
Klass: En beskrivning av en samling objekt som delar struktur, beteendemönster och attribut

Problemområde: Den del av en ordning som administreras, övervakas eller styrs av ett system
Användningsområde: Den organisation som administrerar, övervakar eller styr ett problemområde, 
[[Problemområde: Systemets syfte, administrerad, övervakad, styrd, systemet modellerar], [Användningsområde: Untyttjas av användare [Användare <-> datasystem]]]
e.g. lönesystemet: Användningsområde: personalavdelning, problemområdet: anställda, deras kontrakt och deras arbetstider

-> Huvuduppgift att modellera det som systemet ska administrera, övervaka eller styra
->Modellera hur systemet samverkar med användare inom användningsområdet (Utpeka användargrupper och förstå användningen av systemet)

Problemområdet och systemets modell av problemområdet måste överensstämma fullständigt, systemets modell organiserad i enlighet med hur problemområdets struktur uppfattas (Både för att förstå systemets omgivning och föra att lära sig hur ett använtbart sätt ska representera för systemets användare)
Oenighet i praktiken (Användare och systemutvecklare tolkar på olika sätt, användare oeniga inbördes), växling mellan nutid och framtid (existerande och nya)
System: En samling av komponenter som implementerar modelleringskrav, funktioner och gränssnitt)

4 allmänna principer för analys och design (som metod baseras på):
- Modellera systemets omgivning
- Betona arkitekturövervägande
- Återanvänd mönster som inrymmer etablerade designideer
- Anpasssa metoden till varje utvecklingssituation/till enskilda projekt
Resultat: Ett analysdokument och ett designdokument

Reflect the interactions of the requirements specification, no less and no more.
Requirements  happening "outside" the actor are dropped, since no interaction between actor (cachier) and the system, (e.g. The customer arrives and asks to rent a car., The customer describes the desired car.)
A system operation shall have a name that starts with a verb, and describes what is done. (e.g. The cashier registers the customer’s wishes., The program tells that such a car is available. -> searchMatchingCar)

Encapsulation:
visibility: public / private, static, final (it is safest to consider the final modifier to be part of the public interface because the final value could not be changed.)  

High Cohesion:
A class shall represent one single abstraction, which is clearly identified by the class name. The class shall have knowledge about that abstraction and not about anything else and perform tasks related to that abstraction, not to anything else.

Low Coupling:
As few dependencies/interaction in class diagrams as possible in the program. No strict maximum allowed number, but remove dependencies that can be avoided
Apply architecture pattern with each package for each layer

MVC (Model-View-Controller) architecture pattern:
Controller: + systemOperation1(), + systemOperation2(), etc
…

Layered-MVC:
Main method: start the program, not related to any applicational layer.
Ccontroller layer -> model layer (Model shall only be called by controller)
dbhandler/integration layer -> database layer (data shall only be called by dbhandler)
controller layer -> dbhandler layer (Layers may be bypassed. It is for example perfectly fine to call dbhandler directly from controller, cannot bypass from view to other layer)

DTO (Data Transfer Object) Design Pattern: grouping a long parameter list means a large public interface with big risk for change
Read-only and immutable (only get methods). Cannot change state (no history), only a snapshot of an entity at particular instance

1. Design one system operation at a time, translate each system operation from SSD into each interaction diagram (sequential/communication diagram), with time/execution flow
2. Follow design pattern guidelines
  - DM helps to find new classes that can be introduced. If the DM is changed, all involved parties must agree on that change.
  - Favor objects over primitive data and avoid static members, since neither primitive data nor static members are object oriented. When using these, the entire object concept is completely ignored, and the prime tool (objects) to handle encapsulation, cohesion and coupling is thrown away.

Evaluation:
Encapsulation:
  - All methods in searchMatchingCar are public, not ideal but acceptable early in design.
  - Public methods are necessary because layers must communicate and the system still has few methods.
  - All fields are private, which is considered good encapsulation practice.
Cohesion (Each class performs exactly its intended responsibility):
  - Main: starts the program.
  - View: delegates calls to the controller.
  - Controller: executes a system operation that triggers the search in CarRegistry.
  - CarRegistry: contains only the search method.
  - CarDTO: contains no methods (pure data holder).
Coupling:
  - Dependencies follow the expected layer structure: View -> Controller -> DBHandler. (unidirectional, follow layer pattern)
  - Main is allowed to depend on classes in other layers because its role is to initialize the system.
  - Coupling in Main is low since it references only one class per layer.
  - Excessive references within the same layer would indicate too high coupling, but that is not the case here.
  - Overall cohesion is high: every class focuses on one task.

Spider-in-the-web class: A central class (often the Controller) becomes overly connected to many peripheral classes.
Fix by reducing its associations and letting peripheral classes communicate directly.
Too much primitive data: Excessive use of primitive parameters instead of proper objects/Long parameter lists or many attributes suggest missing abstractions
Unwarranted static methods or fields: Static members should only exist for strong, justified reasons.

Too few classes: A model with only one or very few classes often has poor cohesion.
Each class should represent one responsibility; too few classes suggests overloaded classes.
Too few layers: A missing layer (View, Controller, Model, Startup, Integration) requires justification. Names may vary, but roles must exist. Missing layers makes responsibility separation unclear.
Too few methods: Even if existing methods have high cohesion, some required system tasks may simply be missing. If functionality isn’t implemented, new methods must be added.
Data appears out of nothing: a method cannot be called with parameters the caller cannot possibly know.
Calling an object without a reference: An object must have a reference to another before making a call to it. The design must show how the reference was obtained.
Wrong message numbering: Using sequential unrelated numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) suggests unclear causality. Must be: Call 1 -> calls 1.1 -> calls 1.1.1, etc. when chaining calls
Objects not named when required: Any object appearing more than once in a communication diagram needs a name. Otherwise unclear reference to the same instance

Erroneous constructor: Constructor must:
 - Have the same name as the class.
 - Return the class type.
 - Have the <<create>> stereotype in design diagrams.

Too large class diagram: Can become unreadable if overly detailed or too condensed.
- Split into multiple smaller diagrams.
- Remove unnecessary details (e.g., DTOs, private members).
- Full class design must still exist somewhere for coding.

Too large communication diagram: Becomes messy when too many system operations are included/too many alternative flows are shown at once.
Split into multiple diagrams for clarity.
Implementation of each system operation from interaction diagram + test the relevant parts

One layer -> One package with files, Structured package naming hierarchy
Utility classes (string parsing/file handling) does not belong to any layer and are placed in a separate package called util.

Package name: reversed internet domain -> product name -> specific package, se.kth.iv1350.rentcar.model
Class/interface: Full descriptive name, PascalCase
Method: Full description, camelCase
Variable/Field/Parameter: full description/camelCase
Constant (final static field): All uppercase, separated by underscore, MILES_PER_KM

Logical behavior of a class/method, not internal/physical level mechanism
method behavior, parameters, and return values
Avoid comments inside methods -> signal to refactor long methods

Code smell: Poor design, must be removed through refactoring
Refactoring: Improve code quality, remove code smell without changing behavior
Duplicated code: Severe, error-prone, inefficiency and maintenance disaster

Long method: Its name cannot fully explain it
-> Split into smaller methods, reducing method calls does not meaningfully improve performance
Large class: Low class cohesion -> splitting class with related fields

Long parameter list: 
1. Replace primitive parameters with objects -> improve cohesion, encapsulation and maintainability
2. Remove unnecessary parameters by letting method obtain data instead of parameter passing

Excessive Use of Primitive Variables/Primitive Obsession:
1. Group primitives using objects instead of excessive primitive fields -> improve cohesion, ensure valid data, encapsulation, and overall design quality
2. Never use arrays to store unrelated primitive values, objects so each piece of data has a clear, meaningful name.
3. Use enumerations instead of strings/integers -> avoid errors and make code meanings explicit

Meaningless names: All declared program elements must have meaningful names. (packages, classes, interfaces, methods, fields, parameters, local variables, etc.)
1. Avoid 1‑letter identifiers (p for Person), except abstraction is naturally 1 letter (coordinate x, loop variable i, j, k)
2. Short-lived variables during swap as tmp/temp
3. fromAccount/toAccount instead of account1/account2
4. long names -> clarity

Anonymous values/Literals: Hard to understand and maintain, use named constants, Named values are safer
No numeric values, use expression (CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECS * MILLIS_PER_SECOND)
String using String.format
Method for if-statements -> "if (isUnixEol(ch))" instead of "if (c == 10)"

Complicated Flow Control: Poorly structured/deeply nested if statements with unecessary flags -> hard to understand logic
Use guard statements
Incomplete comments: Every public class, method, etc. must have a Javadoc comment, including setts and getters
Excessive comments: Only Javadoc comments should be used, If extra comments seem necessary, the code is likely too complex or has low cohesion.

Comments written too late: Write comments together with the code (or before), early commenting clarifies intent and ensures comments remain useful and accurate.
Writing comments last makes it burdensome and more likely to be skipped.

Design mistakes introduced during coding: Even if avoided in design, mistakes can reappear in implementation.
e.g. Using primitives where objects should be used, Overuse of `static`, Placing input/output outside the view layer.

Ongoing during programming, after each system operation developed
Unit tests verify that individual pieces of code (methods) produces intended behavior in isolation.

Reusable functionality, controls program flow -> calling application code at correct times
Each test method runs with fresh setup and cleanup, and JUnit executes them by following a standard pattern: prepare objects, define the expected result, call the method under test, and compare expected with actual.
NetBeans, IntelliJ, Maven
@Test -> Marks a method as test method, method will run when test suite is executed
@Disabled("<reason>"): Skips the annotated test, useful for tests not yet implemented or temporarily turned off.
@BeforeEach: Runs before every test method, Used to prepare or reset test state.
@AfterEach: Runs after every test method, Used for cleanup tasks.
@BeforeAll: Runs once before all tests in the class. (Expensive setup)
@AfterAll: Runs once after all tests in the class. Used for global cleanup (also usually static).
fail("explanation"): Forces the test to fail unconditionally at code locations that should never be reached.
assertTrue(condition, "explanation"): Passes if the condition is true.
assertFalse(condition, "explanation"): Passes if the condition is false.
assertEquals(expected, actual, "explanation"): Passes if expected and actual are equal, Works for any Java type.
assertNull(object, "explanation"): passes if the object is null.
assertNotNull(object, "explanation"): Passes if the object is **not null
Writing unit tests early: Improve them over time rather than delaying until too burdensome to write.
Lots of tests, never rely on manual testing and keep all tests (disable them instead of deleting) so your test suite continuously grows and remains useful over time.
Tests for every known bug: Discover bug -> create failing test before fix code, ensuring every known failure condition is permanently covered by a test.
Not over-designed: Write simpler, flexible code and small hacks in tests, not same level of structure as production code

Organization: Place test classes in the same package as production code, parallel test directory. Each class should have a corresponding test class named with "Test" appended, with test methods starting with "test" and containing only a few assertions to keep results clear and easy to interpret.
Independent and self-evaluating: Tests run with single command, automatic self-evaluate, never depend on test execution order, should not produce behavior to System.out

Test public, protected, package private, avoid private and trivial methods (setters/getters)
Cover branches, boundary cases, invalid inputs and correct failure behavior
Input from files, databases, complex object structures: create -> test -> clean up
void methods/methods changing state -> test observable effects through related operations (use other functions) -> verify correct behavior

Complex dependencies: Higher-layer classes depend on lower-layer components -> Test entire stack and identify the lowest failing cases. Test cases written bottom-up (from no dependencies -> moving upward)
Production code MUST NOT be modified to simplify testing

Too many assertions in the same test method: Place as few assertions as possible in each test method—ideally one—because clearer, smaller tests are easier to name and understand, and they allow more assertions to run before a failure stops execution.
